channel.title: Zaika Worlds
channel.description: Cook famous dishes from Pakistan and India, plus favourites from around the world, with big photos and step by step methods.

item.title: Chicken Biryani
item.description: Biryani is not just food, it is a feast. Marinate the chicken in yoghurt and spices, boil the rice halfway, then put it on dum, masala below, rice on top, and the colour in between that makes every bite special.

item.title: Beef Nihari
item.description: Nihari is not fast food, it is food of patience. Cook the meat on low heat for hours, until it falls off the bone and the gravy takes on its deep colour and flavour.

item.title: Chicken Karahi
item.description: The secret of karahi is fresh tomatoes and high heat. No onion is needed, the tomato water itself becomes the masala, and ginger and green chillies at the end complete it.

item.title: Daal Fry (Tadka Daal)
item.description: Daal is every home's daily food, but the tadka makes it special. Boil the daal until soft, then temper cumin, garlic and whole red chillies in ghee, the aroma alone is enough.

item.title: Chapli Kabab
item.description: Chapli kebab means flat, soft and spicy. Mix tomato, pomegranate seeds and whole spices into the mince, flatten it by hand, then fry both sides on a tawa.

item.title: Chicken Tikka
item.description: Good tikka comes from marination. Keep chicken in yoghurt, red chilli and garam masala for at least 1 hour, then grill on high heat, lightly charred outside, juicy inside.

item.title: Halwa Puri Nashta
item.description: Halwa puri is not breakfast, it is a tradition. Puffed puri, soft halwa and spiced chickpeas, the combination of all three is the soul of this breakfast.

item.title: Punjabi Samosa
item.description: A samosa lives in its crisp pastry and spiced potato. Knead the flour firm, mix garam masala and coriander into the potato, then fry on low heat, the pastry will be golden and crisp.

item.title: Bun Kebab
item.description: Bun kebab is Karachi's identity. Fry shami kebabs on a tawa, place them in a bun, add onion, tomato and tamarind chutney, every bite has the perfect balance of masala and chutney.

item.title: Gulab Jamun
item.description: Gulab jamun turn soft when the khoya is good and the syrup is lightly warm. Fry the jamuns on low heat, then put them in syrup for 1 hour, they will drink the syrup and swell.

item.title: Gajar Ka Halwa
item.description: Gajar ka halwa needs patience. Cook the carrots in milk on low heat; when the milk dries, add ghee and sugar, and finish with khoya and almonds, the best winter aroma.

item.title: Mango Lassi
item.description: Mango lassi is summer's answer. Take ripe, sweet mangoes, add cold yoghurt and cardamom aroma, 1 minute in the blender, and comfort in a glass.

item.title: Margherita Pizza
item.description: Margherita pizza is proof that simple food can be extraordinary. It was made famous in Naples, where a hot oven, a thin crust, bright tomato sauce and good mozzarella do all the work. The colours are said to echo the Italian flag, red tomato, white mozzarella and green basil, and the flavour is clean and fresh rather than heavy. This version uses a dough that rests long enough to become light and chewy, a sauce that is barely cooked, and a very hot oven so the crust blisters in minutes. Take time with the dough and the heat, and the pizza will taste like a pizzeria pizza, even from a home oven.

item.title: Spaghetti Carbonara
item.description: Real carbonara has no cream. It comes from Rome, and its sauce is made only from eggs, pecorino cheese, black pepper and the fat from guanciale or pancetta, mixed with hot pasta until it turns glossy and silky. The trick is heat control. The pan must be hot enough to cook the eggs gently into a sauce, but never so hot that they scramble. Work quickly, use pasta water to loosen the sauce, and serve at once. Once you learn the timing, this becomes one of the fastest and most comforting pasta dishes you can make, with only a handful of ingredients and a depth of flavour that tastes far more complex than it is.

item.title: Sushi
item.description: Sushi is about rice first and fish second. In Japan, the rice is seasoned with vinegar, sugar and salt, fanned cool, and handled gently so every grain stays separate and glossy. This home version makes salmon and cucumber rolls, the kind that are easiest to learn, with nori on the outside, rice in the middle, and a neat line of filling. Use sushi grade salmon, keep your hands wet, and roll firmly but gently. The first roll may look uneven, and that is normal. By the third roll, the shape, the cut and the confidence all come together, and the result tastes fresh, clean and far better than shop bought sushi that has sat in a fridge.

item.title: Ramen
item.description: Ramen is comfort in a bowl, and a good home version does not need a broth that simmers all day. This chicken ramen builds flavour quickly, with garlic, ginger and spring onions fried in sesame oil, chicken stock enriched with soy and miso, and noodles cooked separately so the broth stays clear and the noodles stay springy. The egg is the finishing touch, soft in the middle and seasoned by the broth as you eat. Set out the toppings in small bowls and let everyone build their own bowl, hot broth last, so the noodles do not sit and soften. It is fast, warming and deeply satisfying, and it tastes like care, not like a shortcut.

item.title: Tacos al Pastor
item.description: Tacos al pastor began with Lebanese shawarma cooking in Mexico City, and it became something entirely Mexican, pork marinated in dried chillies and achiote, cooked until charred at the edges, and served in warm corn tortillas with pineapple, onion and coriander. The marinade does the heavy work, so give it time, even 30 minutes makes a difference, and overnight is better. Cook the pork hot and fast so it chars without drying out, warm the tortillas over an open flame or in a dry pan, and keep the toppings simple. The sweet pineapple against the smoky, spiced pork is the whole point, so do not skip it, and serve with lime and salsa on the side.

item.title: Pozole
item.description: Pozole is a celebration soup from Mexico, made with hominy, the large white corn kernels that puff and soften in a long simmer, and pork that cooks until it shreds with a spoon. The red version gets its colour and depth from dried guajillo and ancho chillies, blended smooth and stirred into the broth, while the toppings stay fresh and crisp, shredded cabbage, radish, onion, oregano and lime. It takes time, but most of that time is unattended, and the pot feeds a crowd. Cook it on a weekend, keep the broth rich and the toppings separate, and let everyone finish their own bowl at the table.

item.title: Pad Thai
item.description: Pad thai is Thailand's most famous noodle dish, and its magic is balance, sweet, sour, salty and a little heat, all in one hot wok. The sauce is made from tamarind, fish sauce, palm sugar and chilli, and it coats rice noodles that are soaked, not boiled, so they stay springy instead of soft. Prawns, egg, bean sprouts and chives go in quickly, at high heat, and the dish is finished with crushed peanuts, lime and extra sprouts on the side. Have everything ready before you start, because once the wok is hot, the cooking takes only a few minutes, and that speed is what keeps the noodles from turning mushy.

item.title: Peking Duck
item.description: Peking duck is one of China's great celebration dishes, famous for skin so crisp it shatters, and meat that stays juicy underneath. The secret is drying the skin and glazing it before roasting, so the fat renders out and the skin turns a deep lacquered red gold. This home version uses an overnight rest in the fridge to dry the skin, a simple maltose and vinegar glaze, and a hot oven, followed by a rest before carving. Serve it the traditional way, in thin mandarin pancakes with hoisin sauce, spring onion and cucumber, and let everyone assemble their own. It is a project, not a weeknight dinner, and it is worth every minute.

item.title: Dim Sum
item.description: Dim sum means food that touches the heart, and it is meant to be shared, small bamboo steamers arriving at the table one after another, each with a different bite inside. This home version makes two classics, prawn har gow with translucent wrappers, and pork and prawn siu mai with open tops, both steamed until just cooked and served hot. The wrappers need a light touch and a little patience, but the filling is simple, and the steaming is quick. Make them with help, one person filling, one person folding, and keep the finished dumplings covered so they do not dry out. Serve with tea, as in Cantonese yum cha, and let the meal stretch out slowly.

item.title: Coq au Vin
item.description: Coq au vin is classic French comfort food, chicken braised slowly in red wine until it falls from the bone, with mushrooms, pearl onions and bacon in a sauce that tastes of the wine without tasting alcoholic. It comes from Burgundy, where the wine is part of the cooking, not just an accompaniment, and the long gentle braise is what makes the chicken tender and the sauce rich. Brown the chicken well first, because that colour becomes flavour, then let the pot do the work in the oven. Serve it with mashed potatoes or crusty bread, and give the sauce a final taste for salt and a little butter to make it shine.

item.title: Bouillabaisse
item.description: Bouillabaisse comes from Marseille, where fishermen made soup from the fish that did not sell, and it is now one of France's most loved celebration dishes. The broth is the star, built from fish stock, tomatoes, fennel, orange peel, saffron and olive oil, and the fish and shellfish cook in it for only a few minutes, so they stay tender. Serve it in two parts if you can, broth strained into bowls and fish on a platter, with rouille, a saffron garlic mayonnaise, spread on toasted bread. It sounds grand, but the method is simple, make a good broth, add the fish in the right order, and do not overcook it.

item.title: Seafood Paella
item.description: Paella comes from Valencia in Spain, where it is cooked outdoors in a wide shallow pan, and the rice, not the seafood, is the real star. Saffron gives it the golden colour, a good stock gives it flavour, and the last few minutes of cooking, left undisturbed, create socarrat, the crisp toasted layer of rice at the bottom that everyone fights over. Use short grain bomba rice if you can, spread it in an even layer, and resist stirring once the stock goes in. Serve it in the pan, in the middle of the table, with lemon wedges, and let everyone dig in together.

item.title: Beef Pho
item.description: Pho is Vietnam's most famous soup, and its heart is a clear broth that tastes of charred onion and ginger, star anise, cinnamon, cloves and fish sauce, simmered gently with beef bones until it is rich but never cloudy. The noodles cook separately, the beef is sliced paper thin and cooks in the hot broth as it is poured over, and the bowl is finished at the table with bean sprouts, Thai basil, coriander, lime and chilli. It takes time, but the work is mostly waiting and skimming, and the result is a bowl that is light, fragrant and deeply comforting, nothing like a heavy stew.

item.title: Poutine
item.description: Poutine comes from Quebec in Canada, and it is gloriously simple, hot crisp fries, fresh cheese curds that squeak when you bite them, and a rich brown gravy poured over the top so the curds just start to melt. The fries must be crisp enough to hold the gravy without going soggy in a minute, so double frying is worth it, and the gravy must be piping hot, because it is the heat that softens the curds. Serve it at once, in a bowl, with a fork, and eat it while the fries are still crisp at the edges and the gravy is pooling at the bottom.

item.title: Bobotie
item.description: Bobotie is South Africa's beloved baked mince dish, with roots in Cape Malay cooking, where spiced mince is sweetened with fruit, enriched with soaked bread, and baked under a golden egg custard topping with bay leaves. The flavour is warm and gently sweet, curry powder, turmeric, chutney, raisins and apricot all working together, and the texture is soft and comforting, somewhere between a savoury bake and a light meatloaf. Serve it with yellow rice, chutney and a simple salad, and let the sweet and savoury balance do the talking. It is an ideal make ahead dish for a crowd, because it reheats beautifully and tastes even better the next day.

item.title: Moussaka
item.description: Moussaka is Greece's great layered bake, soft aubergine, a rich tomato and lamb or beef mince sauce scented with cinnamon, and a thick bechamel top that turns golden in the oven. It takes a little time, because each layer is cooked separately before the dish is assembled, but that is what gives it its structure and flavour, and it is best made ahead and rested, so the layers set and slice cleanly. Serve it warm, in squares, with a simple salad, and do not rush the resting time. It is a Sunday dish, generous and comforting, and it feeds a table happily.

item.title: Hummus
item.description: Good hummus is all about texture, silky, light and whipped, never grainy or heavy. It comes from the Levant, where chickpeas, tahini, lemon and garlic are blended with ice water until the dip turns pale and fluffy, then finished with olive oil, paprika and whole chickpeas. The secret is to blend the tahini first, on its own, until it is completely smooth, and to use warm chickpeas, or chickpeas with their skins rubbed off, for the smoothest result. Serve it as part of a mezze spread, with warm pitta, olives and salad, and let everyone scoop and share.

item.title: Falafel
item.description: Real falafel is made from raw soaked chickpeas, never tinned or cooked chickpeas, and that is what gives it a light, fluffy inside and a crisp, craggy crust. The chickpeas are ground coarse with onion, garlic, parsley, coriander and cumin, rested so the mixture holds together, then shaped and fried until deep golden. Serve them in warm pitta with salad and tahini sauce, or as part of a mezze spread with hummus. The mixture can be made ahead and chilled, and the falafel fry in minutes, so they are perfect for a crowd, as long as you do not crowd the pan.

item.title: Feijoada
item.description: Feijoada is Brazil's national dish, a rich black bean stew with a mix of pork, sausage and smoked meats, cooked slowly until the beans are creamy and the meats are tender. It is traditionally served on Saturdays, as a long family lunch, with white rice, sauteed collard greens, farofa, toasted cassava flour, and orange slices to cut the richness. It takes time, and it feeds a crowd, so cook a big pot, keep the accompaniments simple, and let the meal stretch out. Soak the beans overnight, brown the meats well, and give the pot a long, gentle simmer, and the result is deeply satisfying.

item.title: Aussie Meat Pie
item.description: The Aussie meat pie is an icon, handheld, golden and eaten at football games, bakeries and kitchen tables all over Australia. Inside a crisp shortcrust base and a flaky puff pastry lid is a rich beef filling, slow cooked with onion, tomato, Worcestershire sauce and a little Vegemite for depth, thick enough to hold its shape when the pie is cut, but juicy enough to need tomato sauce on top. Make the filling ahead and cool it fully, because warm filling melts the pastry, then bake until the lid is deep golden. Serve it hot, with tomato sauce, and eat it with your hands, the Australian way.
